overview: The Garamantes built an urban society in the Fazzan region of the central Sahara. Archaeology reveals towns, cultivated oases and underground water systems, challenging older portrayals of the inhabitants as merely scattered desert nomads.

items.text: Networks of underground channels and access shafts tapped groundwater for irrigation. These systems are known as foggaras.
Local cultivation included grains, pulses, grapes and figs. Farming supported settled communities in a landscape without a large river.
Imported wine and olive oil accompanied local produce, indicating connections with markets outside the oasis region.
The excavation-based account links irrigation maintenance with coerced labor and slave acquisition. Engineering achievements should be understood alongside the people who bore their costs.
Survey identified several substantial towns and many smaller settlements. Garama was one center within a larger settled landscape.

sources.title: David Keys, Kingdom of the Sands, Archaeology, March/April 2004
